summary.text: The Event Horizon Telescope is a telescope array made from a global network of radio telescopes.

It combines data from several very-long-baseline interferometry stations around Earth, which gives it enough angular resolution to observe objects the size of a supermassive black hole's event horizon.
Its collaboration published the first image of a black hole, at the center of galaxy Messier 87, in 2019.

facts.label: Collaboration size
facts.value: Over 300 members working in over 20 countries and regions

facts.label: Effective aperture
facts.value: The diameter of the entire planet

items.prompt: Far-apart stations record signals on hard drives, together with time signals from atomic clocks. Why are the drives then shipped to one place?

options.label: To store them safely in one vault for later
To be synchronized and combined into one image
To compare the clocks against the local weather
To print out the radio waves onto paper

items.explain: Each antenna records digital data with precise clock time, and the drives are brought to a central location to be synchronized and processed into an image.

items.prompt: Radio antennas thousands of kilometres apart are linked by VLBI. What do they behave like?

options.label: A group of unrelated small separate telescopes
A single large dish bolted to the ground
One big mirror that must be steered by hand
A virtual telescope as wide as the planet

items.explain: VLBI lets independent antennas act as a phased array, a virtual telescope pointed electronically whose effective aperture is the diameter of the planet.

items.prompt: Some of the data from the 2017 campaign could not be processed until December. What held it up?

options.label: The South Pole drives could not be flown out during winter
The hard drives were lost in transit
The computers were not yet built
The telescopes were busy with other targets

items.explain: No flights run in or out of the South Pole during austral winter, so the full data set waited for the South Pole Telescope's shipment.

items.prompt: How did the first black hole image serve as a check on Einstein's theory?

options.label: It showed the black hole shining like a star
It showed no sign of the black hole at all
It matched the predicted dark shadow caused by bent and captured light
It disproved the idea that light can bend

items.explain: Relativity predicts a dark shadow-like region from gravitational bending and capture of light, and the observed image is consistent with it.

items.prompt: Turning radio data into a picture takes heavy math. How did the team check that the picture was reliable?

options.label: Four independent teams each made images
They trusted a single algorithm completely
They drew it by hand from memory
They only used the brightest data points

items.explain: Four independent teams created images to assess the reliability of the results.

items.prompt: The southern part of the ring in the M87 image was brighter than the rest. What did astronomers conclude from it?

options.label: The black hole is shrinking
The black hole spins clockwise as seen from Earth
The black hole has no spin at all
The black hole is pointing away from Earth

items.explain: The enhanced brightness comes from relativistic beaming of approaching jet emission, so the black hole spins clockwise as seen from Earth.
